newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU finance ministers to meet on EMU on Sunday.
newsitem.headline: EU finance ministers to meet on EMU on Sunday.

text.p: European Union finance ministers will meet for an unusual session on Sunday evening in Luxembourg to discuss economic and monetary union (EMU), an EU diplomat said on Wednesday.
But he stressed the meeting had been planned for some time and was not directly related to current concerns over German and French efforts to qualify for the single currency.
"It has been in the pipeline for some time," he said.
The earlier start has been called because part of Monday's regular meeting will be taken up by the annual two-hour session between finance ministers and the European Investment Bank.

But it was clear that ministers would discuss outstanding EMU issues including the stability pact and the post-EMU exchange rate mechanism, issues that must be formally agreed at the EU summit in Amsterdam on June 16-17.
"I think people expect to see (German Finance Minister Theo) Waigel and a new French finance minister," the diplomat said.

He noted that European Commission president Jacques Santer considered the meeting important enough to urge the Dutch EU presidency not to hold a special foreign ministers meeting at the same to discuss ongoing EU treaty negotiations.
Santer wanted to attend the finance ministers meeting, the diplomat said.

Europe's plans for a single currency to begin on January 1, 1999 have been shaken over the past weeks, first by German plans to revalue gold reserves to help meet EMU criteria and secondly by the election of a Socialist French government.
Waigel backed down in a confrontation with the Bundesbank on Tuesday, agreeing that the gold revaluation -- criticised as an accounting trick -- would take place next year.
The French Socialists, however, ran a campaign against the austerity programme launched to help France meet the EMU criteria and have said they want the stability pact agreement to be re-opened.

Market analysts say the difficulties faced by France and Germany in qualifying for EMU have given the bloc a stark choice between starting on time with a weaker-than-planned currency or delaying the project.
